**Commentary on Surah 98 (Al-Bayyinah), by al-Qurtubi, from *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an*, verses 1–3 (part 1 of 2)**

The commentary (*tafsir*) on the surah "Lam yakun" (The Clear Evidence). It is Makki (revealed in Makkah) according to Yahya ibn Salam, and Madani (revealed in Madinah) according to Ibn Abbas and the majority of scholars. It has nine verses [[In our copies of the Mushaf: eight verses. In al-Alusi's *Tafsir*: its verses are nine according to the Basrans and eight according to others.]]. A hadith concerning its virtues has been related, but it is not authentic. We have related it from Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Abd Allah al-Hadrami, who said: Abu Abd al-Rahman ibn Numayr said to me: "Go to Abu al-Haytham al-Khashshab and write down from him, for he has written." So I went to him, and he said: Malik ibn Anas narrated to us, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu al-Darda', who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If people knew what is in [Lam yakuni alladhina kafaru min ahli al-kitab], they would neglect their families and wealth, so learn it." A man from Khuza'ah said: "What is its reward, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "No hypocrite will ever recite it, nor a servant in whose heart there is doubt about Allah. By Allah, the angels brought near (to Allah) recite it, since Allah created the heavens and the earth, and they never tire of reciting it. No servant recites it except that Allah sends to him angels who guard him in his religion and his worldly life, and they pray for him for forgiveness and mercy." Al-Hadrami said: "So I came to Abu Abd al-Rahman ibn Numayr and recited this hadith to him, and he said: 'This has spared us its burden, so do not return to it.'"

Ibn al-Arabi said: Ishaq ibn Bishr al-Kahili related from Malik ibn Anas, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu al-Darda', from the Prophet ﷺ: "If people knew what is in [Lam yakun alladhina kafaru], they would neglect their families and wealth, and they would learn it" [[In the first narration of the hadith, p. 138: "so learn it."]]. This is a false hadith. The authentic hadith is what is related from Anas: that the Prophet ﷺ said to Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "Allah has commanded me to recite to you [Lam yakuni alladhina kafaru]." He said: "And He named me to you?" He said: "Yes," and he wept. I say: al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded it. In it is a point of jurisprudence (*fiqh*): a scholar reciting to a student. Some have said: the Prophet ﷺ recited to Ubayy only to teach people humility, so that no one would feel disdain for learning and reciting from one who is lower than him in rank. It has also been said: Ubayy was quicker than others at taking up the words of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so by reciting to him he wished that he would take up his words and recite as he heard them and teach others. In it is also a great virtue for Ubayy, since Allah commanded His Messenger to recite to him.

Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: Ahmad ibn al-Haytham ibn Khalid narrated to us, saying: Ali ibn al-Ja'd narrated to us, saying: Ikrimah narrated to us, from Asim, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, who said: In the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "The son of Adam, if he were given a valley of wealth, he would seek a second; and if he were given two valleys of wealth, he would seek a third. Nothing fills the belly of the son of Adam except dust, and Allah accepts the repentance of whoever repents." Ikrimah said: Asim recited to me (*Lam yakun*) thirty verses, and this was among them. Abu Bakr said: This is false according to the people of knowledge, because the two recitations of Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr are connected to Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and in them this that is mentioned in (*Lam yakun*) is not recited, which is known from the hadith of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and that it is from the words of the Messenger (peace be upon him), not something he related from the Lord of the worlds in the Qur'an. What two reliable narrators relate, along with which there is consensus, is more firmly established than what one narrator relates that opposes the position of the majority.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The disbelievers among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to desist until there came to them clear evidence: a messenger from Allah reciting purified scriptures, in which are upright books.﴾

His saying, the Exalted: "Lam yakuni alladhina kafaru" is the reading of the common people and the script of the Mushaf. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Lam yakuni al-mushrikuna wa ahlu al-kitabi munfakkina," and this is a reading in the manner of interpretation (*tafsir*). Ibn al-Arabi said: It is permissible in the context of explanation, but not in the context of recitation (*tilawah*). The Prophet ﷺ, in a narration of the Sahih, recited "fatalliquhunna li-qubuli 'iddatihinna" [So divorce them at the beginning of their waiting period], and that is an explanation. The recitation is what is in the script of the Mushaf.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿from the People of the Book﴾ means the Jews and the Christians.

"Wa al-mushrikin" (and the polytheists) is in the genitive position, conjoined to "ahl al-kitab." Ibn Abbas said: The People of the Book are the Jews who were in Yathrib, namely Qurayzah, al-Nadir, and Banu Qaynuqa'. The polytheists are those who were in Makkah and around it, and in Madinah and those around it, namely the polytheists of Quraysh.

"Munfakkin" means: ceasing from their disbelief and turning away from it.

"Hatta ta'tiyahum" means: until the clear evidence came to them, that is, Muhammad ﷺ. It has also been said: the cessation (*intiha'*) is reaching the limit, meaning they would not have reached the end of their lives and died until the clear evidence came to them. So disengagement (*infikak*) in this sense means cessation. It has also been said: "munfakkin" means "departing," meaning their term would not end until a messenger came to them. The Arabs say: "ma infakakta af'alu kadha," meaning "I have not ceased doing so," and "ma infakka fulanun qa'iman," meaning "so-and-so has not ceased standing." The root of *fakk* is opening, and from it come "fakk al-kitab" (opening a book), "fakk al-khalkhal" (unfastening an anklet), and "fakk al-salim" [[As in some copies of the original: "fakk al-salim." In others: "fakk al-salim wa huwa qal Tarafah," with a blank after "wa huwa." And in al-Tha'labi's *Tafsir*: "wa fakk al-salim wa hiya huruf al-fatn qal Tarafah." We have not determined the correct reading here.]]. Tarafah said:

"I have sworn that my flank will never cease to be a lining
For a keen sword, thin at its two edges, well-polished."

[[Al-kashh: the side. Al-adb: the sharp sword. Muhannad: sharpened; al-tahnid is sharpening. It is said: a sword is muhannad when it has been worked in the land of India.]]

And Dhu al-Rummah said:

"Lean she-camels that do not cease, except kneeling
On the ground, or we cast them upon a barren land."

[[Al-harajij (plural of harjuj): the long, lean she-camel. Al-khasf: to spend the night without fodder. He says: they do not part from one land to another except by kneeling without fodder.]]

He means: "ma tanfakku munakhah" (they do not cease kneeling), and he added "illa" (except). It has also been said: "munfakkin" means "departing," meaning they would not depart from the world and leave it until the clear evidence came to them. Ibn Kaysan said: That is, the People of the Book were not abandoning the description of Muhammad ﷺ in their scripture until he was sent. When he was sent, they envied him and denied him. This is like His saying: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:89]. For this reason He said: ﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not divide except after clear evidence came to them﴾ [Al-Bayyinah 98:4]... the verse. On this view, His saying "wa al-mushrikin" means that they did not speak ill of Muhammad ﷺ until he was sent, for they used to call him "the trustworthy" (al-Amin), until the clear evidence came to them through his tongue and he was sent to them, and then they became hostile to him. Some linguists said: "munfakkin" means "perishing," from their saying: "infakka sala al-mar'ah" [the pelvic bone of the woman separated], when she gives birth, meaning it separates and does not rejoin, and she perishes. The meaning is: they would not be punished or perish except after the proof had been established against them, by sending messengers and revealing books.

Some said regarding the polytheists: they are among the People of the Book. Among the Jews were those who said: "Uzayr is the son of Allah." Among the Christians were those who said: "Isa is God," and among them were those who said: "He is the son of God," and among them were those who said: "He is the third of three." It has been said: the People of the Book were believers, then they disbelieved after their prophets. And the polytheists were born upon the natural disposition (*fitrah*), then they disbelieved when they reached maturity. For this reason He said: "wa al-mushrikin." It has also been said: "al-mushrikun" is also a description of the People of the Book, because they did not benefit from their scripture and abandoned monotheism. So the Christians are trinitarian, the majority of the Jews are anthropomorphists, and all of this is polytheism. This is like your saying: "The intelligent and the witty came to me," while you mean specific people, describing them with both qualities. So the meaning is: from the People of the Book, the polytheists. It has also been said: the disbelief here is disbelief in the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: those who disbelieved in Muhammad, from among the Jews and Christians who are the People of the Book, and the polytheists, who are the idol-worshippers from among the Arabs and others, and they are those who have no scripture, were not going to desist. Al-Qushayri said: There is a distance in this, because the apparent meaning of His saying "until there comes to them clear evidence, a messenger from Allah" is that this messenger is Muhammad ﷺ. So it would be far-fetched to say: "Those who disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ were not going to desist until Muhammad came to them," unless it is said: he meant: those who disbelieved now in Muhammad, though they had previously held him in high regard, were not going to cease this disbelief until Allah sent Muhammad to them and made the signs clear to them, and then a people would believe. Al-A'mash and Ibrahim read "wa al-mushrikun" in the nominative, conjoined to "alladhina." The first reading is clearer, because in the nominative the two categories appear as though they were not from the People of the Book. In the codex of Ubayy: "fa-ma kana alladhina kafaru min ahli al-kitabi wa al-mushrikuna munfakkin." In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "Lam yakuni al-mushrikuna wa ahlu al-kitabi munfakkin." And this has already been discussed.

"Hatta ta'tiyahumu al-bayyinah" (until the clear evidence came to them): it has been said: "until it came to them." And "al-bayyinah" is Muhammad ﷺ.

"Rasulun min Allah": that is, a messenger (*ba'ith*) from Allah, exalted is His praise. Al-Zajjaj said: "Rasulun" is in the nominative as an apposition (*badal*) to "al-bayyinah." Al-Farra' said: that is, it is a messenger from Allah, or he is a messenger from Allah, because "al-bayyinah" may be masculine, as one says: "bayyinati fulan" (my evidence is so-and-so). In the codex of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud it is "rasulan" in the accusative, as a circumstantial clarification (*qat'*).

"Yatlu": that is, reads. It is said: "talā yatlū tilāwah" (he recited, he recites recitation).

"Suhufan": the plural of *sahifah*, which is the container of what is written.

"Mutahhara": Ibn Abbas said: free from falsehood, doubt, hypocrisy, and misguidance. Qatadah said: free from falsehood. It has also been said: free from lies and doubtful matters, and from disbelief. The meaning is one: that he recites what the pages contain of writing. And this is indicated by the fact that he would recite from memory, not from a book, because he was unlettered (*ummi*), who neither wrote nor read. "Mutahharah" is an attribute of the pages, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿in scrolls honored, exalted, purified﴾ [Abasa 80:13–14]. So "mutahharah" is an attribute of the pages outwardly, and it is an attribute of what is in the pages of the Qur'an. It has also been said: "mutahharah" means it should not be touched except by the purified, as He said in Surah al-Waqi'ah, as its explanation has previously been given [[See vol. 17, p. 225 and following.]]. It has also been said: the purified pages are those that are with Allah in the Mother of the Book, from which were copied what was revealed to the prophets of the scriptures, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Rather, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a preserved tablet﴾ [Al-Buruj 85:21–22]. Al-Hasan said: meaning the purified pages in heaven.

"Fiha kutubun qayyimah": that is, upright, straight, firm, from the saying of the Arabs: "qama yaqumu" when something becomes level and sound. Some scholars said: the pages are the books, so how does He say "suhufin fiha kutubun"? The answer: "kutub" here means rulings (*ahkam*), as Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Allah has decreed: "I will surely overcome"﴾ [Al-Mujadilah 58:21], meaning "decreed" in the sense of "ruled." And the Prophet ﷺ said: "By Allah, I will judge between you two by the Book of Allah," then he ruled by stoning, and the mention of stoning is not written in the Book. So the meaning is: "I will judge between you two by the ruling of Allah, the Exalted." And the poet said:

"And loyalty is not with affliction..."
[[As it stands in the original; we have not found this verse in the sources available to us. Its correct form may be:]]

ومال الولاة بالبلاء فملتم .. إلخ]] فَمِلْتُمُ ... وَمَا ذَاكَ قَالَ اللَّهُ إِذْ هُوَ يَكْتُبُ

"The governors inclined toward affliction, so you inclined ... etc.]] So you inclined ... and that is not so. God said, when He was writing."

وَقِيلَ: الْكُتُبُ الْقَيِّمَةُ: هِيَ الْقُرْآنُ، فَجَعَلَهُ كُتُبًا لِأَنَّهُ يَشْتَمِلُ على أنواع من البيان.

It was said: the upright scriptures (al-kutub al-qayyimah) are the Qur'an, and He made it "scriptures" because it comprises various kinds of clarification.

**Commentary on Surah 98 (Al-Bayyinah), by al-Qurtubi, from *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an*, verses 1–3 (part 1 of 2)**

The commentary (*tafsir*) on the surah "Lam yakun" (The Clear Evidence). It is Makki (revealed in Makkah) according to Yahya ibn Salam, and Madani (revealed in Madinah) according to Ibn Abbas and the majority of scholars. It has nine verses [[In our copies of the Mushaf: eight verses. In al-Alusi's *Tafsir*: its verses are nine according to the Basrans and eight according to others.]]. A hadith concerning its virtues has been related, but it is not authentic. We have related it from Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Abd Allah al-Hadrami, who said: Abu Abd al-Rahman ibn Numayr said to me: "Go to Abu al-Haytham al-Khashshab and write down from him, for he has written." So I went to him, and he said: Malik ibn Anas narrated to us, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu al-Darda', who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If people knew what is in [Lam yakuni alladhina kafaru min ahli al-kitab], they would neglect their families and wealth, so learn it." A man from Khuza'ah said: "What is its reward, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "No hypocrite will ever recite it, nor a servant in whose heart there is doubt about Allah. By Allah, the angels brought near (to Allah) recite it, since Allah created the heavens and the earth, and they never tire of reciting it. No servant recites it except that Allah sends to him angels who guard him in his religion and his worldly life, and they pray for him for forgiveness and mercy." Al-Hadrami said: "So I came to Abu Abd al-Rahman ibn Numayr and recited this hadith to him, and he said: 'This has spared us its burden, so do not return to it.'"

Ibn al-Arabi said: Ishaq ibn Bishr al-Kahili related from Malik ibn Anas, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu al-Darda', from the Prophet ﷺ: "If people knew what is in [Lam yakun alladhina kafaru], they would neglect their families and wealth, and they would learn it" [[In the first narration of the hadith, p. 138: "so learn it."]]. This is a false hadith. The authentic hadith is what is related from Anas: that the Prophet ﷺ said to Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "Allah has commanded me to recite to you [Lam yakuni alladhina kafaru]." He said: "And He named me to you?" He said: "Yes," and he wept. I say: al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded it. In it is a point of jurisprudence (*fiqh*): a scholar reciting to a student. Some have said: the Prophet ﷺ recited to Ubayy only to teach people humility, so that no one would feel disdain for learning and reciting from one who is lower than him in rank. It has also been said: Ubayy was quicker than others at taking up the words of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so by reciting to him he wished that he would take up his words and recite as he heard them and teach others. In it is also a great virtue for Ubayy, since Allah commanded His Messenger to recite to him.

Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: Ahmad ibn al-Haytham ibn Khalid narrated to us, saying: Ali ibn al-Ja'd narrated to us, saying: Ikrimah narrated to us, from Asim, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, who said: In the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "The son of Adam, if he were given a valley of wealth, he would seek a second; and if he were given two valleys of wealth, he would seek a third. Nothing fills the belly of the son of Adam except dust, and Allah accepts the repentance of whoever repents." Ikrimah said: Asim recited to me (*Lam yakun*) thirty verses, and this was among them. Abu Bakr said: This is false according to the people of knowledge, because the two recitations of Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr are connected to Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and in them this that is mentioned in (*Lam yakun*) is not recited, which is known from the hadith of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and that it is from the words of the Messenger (peace be upon him), not something he related from the Lord of the worlds in the Qur'an. What two reliable narrators relate, along with which there is consensus, is more firmly established than what one narrator relates that opposes the position of the majority.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The disbelievers among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to desist until there came to them clear evidence: a messenger from Allah reciting purified scriptures, in which are upright books.﴾

His saying, the Exalted: "Lam yakuni alladhina kafaru" is the reading of the common people and the script of the Mushaf. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Lam yakuni al-mushrikuna wa ahlu al-kitabi munfakkina," and this is a reading in the manner of interpretation (*tafsir*). Ibn al-Arabi said: It is permissible in the context of explanation, but not in the context of recitation (*tilawah*). The Prophet ﷺ, in a narration of the Sahih, recited "fatalliquhunna li-qubuli 'iddatihinna" [So divorce them at the beginning of their waiting period], and that is an explanation. The recitation is what is in the script of the Mushaf.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿from the People of the Book﴾ means the Jews and the Christians.

"Wa al-mushrikin" (and the polytheists) is in the genitive position, conjoined to "ahl al-kitab." Ibn Abbas said: The People of the Book are the Jews who were in Yathrib, namely Qurayzah, al-Nadir, and Banu Qaynuqa'. The polytheists are those who were in Makkah and around it, and in Madinah and those around it, namely the polytheists of Quraysh.

"Munfakkin" means: ceasing from their disbelief and turning away from it.

"Hatta ta'tiyahum" means: until the clear evidence came to them, that is, Muhammad ﷺ. It has also been said: the cessation (*intiha'*) is reaching the limit, meaning they would not have reached the end of their lives and died until the clear evidence came to them. So disengagement (*infikak*) in this sense means cessation. It has also been said: "munfakkin" means "departing," meaning their term would not end until a messenger came to them. The Arabs say: "ma infakakta af'alu kadha," meaning "I have not ceased doing so," and "ma infakka fulanun qa'iman," meaning "so-and-so has not ceased standing." The root of *fakk* is opening, and from it come "fakk al-kitab" (opening a book), "fakk al-khalkhal" (unfastening an anklet), and "fakk al-salim" [[As in some copies of the original: "fakk al-salim." In others: "fakk al-salim wa huwa qal Tarafah," with a blank after "wa huwa." And in al-Tha'labi's *Tafsir*: "wa fakk al-salim wa hiya huruf al-fatn qal Tarafah." We have not determined the correct reading here.]]. Tarafah said:

"I have sworn that my flank will never cease to be a lining
For a keen sword, thin at its two edges, well-polished."

[[Al-kashh: the side. Al-adb: the sharp sword. Muhannad: sharpened; al-tahnid is sharpening. It is said: a sword is muhannad when it has been worked in the land of India.]]

And Dhu al-Rummah said:

"Lean she-camels that do not cease, except kneeling
On the ground, or we cast them upon a barren land."

[[Al-harajij (plural of harjuj): the long, lean she-camel. Al-khasf: to spend the night without fodder. He says: they do not part from one land to another except by kneeling without fodder.]]

He means: "ma tanfakku munakhah" (they do not cease kneeling), and he added "illa" (except). It has also been said: "munfakkin" means "departing," meaning they would not depart from the world and leave it until the clear evidence came to them. Ibn Kaysan said: That is, the People of the Book were not abandoning the description of Muhammad ﷺ in their scripture until he was sent. When he was sent, they envied him and denied him. This is like His saying: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:89]. For this reason He said: ﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not divide except after clear evidence came to them﴾ [Al-Bayyinah 98:4]... the verse. On this view, His saying "wa al-mushrikin" means that they did not speak ill of Muhammad ﷺ until he was sent, for they used to call him "the trustworthy" (al-Amin), until the clear evidence came to them through his tongue and he was sent to them, and then they became hostile to him. Some linguists said: "munfakkin" means "perishing," from their saying: "infakka sala al-mar'ah" [the pelvic bone of the woman separated], when she gives birth, meaning it separates and does not rejoin, and she perishes. The meaning is: they would not be punished or perish except after the proof had been established against them, by sending messengers and revealing books.

Some said regarding the polytheists: they are among the People of the Book. Among the Jews were those who said: "Uzayr is the son of Allah." Among the Christians were those who said: "Isa is God," and among them were those who said: "He is the son of God," and among them were those who said: "He is the third of three." It has been said: the People of the Book were believers, then they disbelieved after their prophets. And the polytheists were born upon the natural disposition (*fitrah*), then they disbelieved when they reached maturity. For this reason He said: "wa al-mushrikin." It has also been said: "al-mushrikun" is also a description of the People of the Book, because they did not benefit from their scripture and abandoned monotheism. So the Christians are trinitarian, the majority of the Jews are anthropomorphists, and all of this is polytheism. This is like your saying: "The intelligent and the witty came to me," while you mean specific people, describing them with both qualities. So the meaning is: from the People of the Book, the polytheists. It has also been said: the disbelief here is disbelief in the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: those who disbelieved in Muhammad, from among the Jews and Christians who are the People of the Book, and the polytheists, who are the idol-worshippers from among the Arabs and others, and they are those who have no scripture, were not going to desist. Al-Qushayri said: There is a distance in this, because the apparent meaning of His saying "until there comes to them clear evidence, a messenger from Allah" is that this messenger is Muhammad ﷺ. So it would be far-fetched to say: "Those who disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ were not going to desist until Muhammad came to them," unless it is said: he meant: those who disbelieved now in Muhammad, though they had previously held him in high regard, were not going to cease this disbelief until Allah sent Muhammad to them and made the signs clear to them, and then a people would believe. Al-A'mash and Ibrahim read "wa al-mushrikun" in the nominative, conjoined to "alladhina." The first reading is clearer, because in the nominative the two categories appear as though they were not from the People of the Book. In the codex of Ubayy: "fa-ma kana alladhina kafaru min ahli al-kitabi wa al-mushrikuna munfakkin." In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "Lam yakuni al-mushrikuna wa ahlu al-kitabi munfakkin." And this has already been discussed.

"Hatta ta'tiyahumu al-bayyinah" (until the clear evidence came to them): it has been said: "until it came to them." And "al-bayyinah" is Muhammad ﷺ.

"Rasulun min Allah": that is, a messenger (*ba'ith*) from Allah, exalted is His praise. Al-Zajjaj said: "Rasulun" is in the nominative as an apposition (*badal*) to "al-bayyinah." Al-Farra' said: that is, it is a messenger from Allah, or he is a messenger from Allah, because "al-bayyinah" may be masculine, as one says: "bayyinati fulan" (my evidence is so-and-so). In the codex of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud it is "rasulan" in the accusative, as a circumstantial clarification (*qat'*).

"Yatlu": that is, reads. It is said: "talā yatlū tilāwah" (he recited, he recites recitation).

"Suhufan": the plural of *sahifah*, which is the container of what is written.

"Mutahhara": Ibn Abbas said: free from falsehood, doubt, hypocrisy, and misguidance. Qatadah said: free from falsehood. It has also been said: free from lies and doubtful matters, and from disbelief. The meaning is one: that he recites what the pages contain of writing. And this is indicated by the fact that he would recite from memory, not from a book, because he was unlettered (*ummi*), who neither wrote nor read. "Mutahharah" is an attribute of the pages, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿in scrolls honored, exalted, purified﴾ [Abasa 80:13–14]. So "mutahharah" is an attribute of the pages outwardly, and it is an attribute of what is in the pages of the Qur'an. It has also been said: "mutahharah" means it should not be touched except by the purified, as He said in Surah al-Waqi'ah, as its explanation has previously been given [[See vol. 17, p. 225 and following.]]. It has also been said: the purified pages are those that are with Allah in the Mother of the Book, from which were copied what was revealed to the prophets of the scriptures, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Rather, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a preserved tablet﴾ [Al-Buruj 85:21–22]. Al-Hasan said: meaning the purified pages in heaven.

"Fiha kutubun qayyimah": that is, upright, straight, firm, from the saying of the Arabs: "qama yaqumu" when something becomes level and sound. Some scholars said: the pages are the books, so how does He say "suhufin fiha kutubun"? The answer: "kutub" here means rulings (*ahkam*), as Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Allah has decreed: "I will surely overcome"﴾ [Al-Mujadilah 58:21], meaning "decreed" in the sense of "ruled." And the Prophet ﷺ said: "By Allah, I will judge between you two by the Book of Allah," then he ruled by stoning, and the mention of stoning is not written in the Book. So the meaning is: "I will judge between you two by the ruling of Allah, the Exalted." And the poet said:

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 98, verse 4:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not become divided except after clear evidence had come to them﴾. That is, from among the Jews and the Christians. He singled out the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab) for division, rather than others, even though they are grouped together with the disbelievers, because knowledge is presumed of them; so when they divide, those who have no scripture are more fitting to be described by this attribute.

(Except after the clear evidence had come to them) That is, the clear proof came to them. What is meant by it is Muhammad (ﷺ), that is, the Qur'an confirming what is in their hands of the Scripture by its description and attributes. This is because they were united upon his prophethood; but when he was sent, they denied his prophethood and became divided. Some of them disbelieved out of insolence (baghy) and envy (hasad), and some of them believed, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they did not become divided except after knowledge had come to them, out of insolence among themselves﴾ [[Qur'an 42:14.]] [al-Shura: 14]. It was also said: the clear evidence (al-bayyinah) is the explanation found in their books that he is a prophet sent. The scholars said: from the beginning of the surah up to His saying ﴿upright scriptures﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5], its ruling concerns those among the People of the Book and the polytheists who believed. As for His saying ﴿and did not become divided﴾, its ruling concerns those among the People of the Book who did not believe after the proofs had been established.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 98, verse 5:

There are three issues in this verse.

The first concerns His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they were not commanded﴾, meaning: these disbelievers were not commanded in the Torah and the Gospel (﴿except to worship God﴾), meaning: to affirm His oneness. The lam in liya'budu (the "lam" of purpose) carries the meaning of (an) (that), as in His saying: "God desires to make clear (liyubayyina) to you" (Qur'an 4:26), meaning "that He make clear." And "They desire to extinguish (liyutfi'u) the light of God" (Qur'an 61:8). And "We have been commanded to submit (linuslima) to the Lord of the worlds" (Qur'an 6:71). And in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "And they were not commanded except that they worship God."

﴿Sincerely devoted to Him in religion﴾, meaning: in worship. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: "Say: I have been commanded to worship God, sincerely devoted to Him in religion" (Qur'an 39:11). In this is evidence for the obligation of intention (niyyah) in acts of worship, for sincerity (ikhlas) is an act of the heart, and it is that by which the Face of God, Exalted is He, and nothing else, is intended.

The second issue concerns His saying: ﴿Upright (hunafa')﴾, meaning: inclining away from all other religions toward the religion of Islam. Ibn Abbas used to say: "Hunafa': upon the religion of Ibrahim, peace be upon him." It has also been said: the hanif is one who is circumcised and performs Hajj; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The lexicographers said: its origin is that he "tahannafa" toward Islam, meaning he inclined toward it.

The third issue concerns His saying: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾, meaning: with its limits, at its times.

(﴿And give the zakah﴾), meaning: they give it at its proper place.

(﴿And that is the upright religion (din al-qayyimah)﴾), meaning: that religion they were commanded with is the upright religion, that is, the straight religion. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning that is the religion of the upright community. Al-qayyimah is an adjective of a deleted noun. Or it is said: the religion of the upright nation (al-ummah al-qayyimah) bi-l-haqq, meaning the one standing upon the truth. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "And that religion is al-qayyim." Al-Khalil said: al-qayyimah is the plural of al-qayyim, and al-qayyim and al-qa'im are one and the same. Al-Farra' said: he attributed the religion to al-qayyimah, which is its adjective, because the two expressions differ. He also said: it is of the type of attributing a thing to itself, and the ha' (feminine marker) entered for praise and emphasis. It has also been said: the ha' refers to the religion (millah) or the law (shari'ah). Muhammad ibn al-Ash'ath al-Talaqani said: al-qayyimah here refers to the scriptures that have been mentioned, and the religion is attributed to them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 98, verses 6–7:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists﴾. "Al-mushrikin" (the polytheists) is in the accusative as a conjunction of "alladhina" (those who), or it may be in the genitive, conjoined to "ahl" (people).

(﴿In the fire of Hell, abiding eternally therein. They are the worst of creation﴾). Nafi' and Ibn Dhakwan read it with a hamza in both places, according to the original form, from their saying "bara'a Allahu al-khalq" (God created creation), and He is "al-Bari'" (the Creator). And He said: ﴿Before We bring it into being﴾ [al-Hadid: 22]. The rest read it without a hamza, and they doubled the ya' as a substitute for it. Al-Farra' said: If "al-bariyyah" is derived from "al-bara" (dust), then its root is without a hamza, and one says from it: "barahu Allah yabruhu bar'an," meaning He created him. Al-Qushayri said: Whoever says that "al-bariyyah" is from "al-bara" (dust) holds that the angels do not enter under this term. It was also said that "al-bariyyah" is from "baraytu al-qalam," meaning I shaped the pen, and in that case the angels would enter under it. But this is a weak opinion, because it would necessitate declaring erroneous the one who reads with a hamza.

His saying, "shar al-bariyyah," means "the worst of creation." It was said that it may be general. Others said: that is, they are the worst of the creation who were in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, just as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 47], meaning over the worlds of your time. It is not far-fetched that among the disbelieving nations before this there were those who were worse than them, such as Pharaoh and the one who hamstrung the she-camel of Salih. Likewise, "khayr al-bariyyah" (the best of creation) is either general, or it means the best of the creation of their time. Those who favour the children of Adam over the angels have used the reading with the hamza as evidence, and the discussion of this has passed in surah "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 1, p. 289, second or third edition.]]. Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The believer is more honoured by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, than some of the angels who are with Him.

Verse 98:8 (al-Qurtubi's commentary)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Their reward﴾, i.e., their recompense.

(With their Lord), i.e., their Creator and their Owner.

(Gardens of) i.e., orchards.

(Eden), i.e., residence (iqamah). The exegetes say: "Gardens of Eden" are the innermost part of Paradise (buṭnan al-jannah), i.e., its middle. It is said: "adana bi-l-makan ya'dinu" [adnan wa-ʿudunan], meaning he resided in the place. And ma'din (mine, origin) of a thing is its center and its established place. Al-A'sha said:

"And if they are called upon to his judgment... they are attributed to a noble one who has become established (qad 'adan)."

(Beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever), they do not depart, and they do not die.

(Allah is pleased with them), i.e., He is pleased with their deeds; thus said Ibn ʿAbbas. (And they are pleased with Him), i.e., they are pleased with the reward of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

(That), i.e., Paradise.

(Is for him who fears his Lord), i.e., who fears his Lord, so he refrains from sins.
